1:
The psalm has no title, and that is disputed. Augustine of Hippo treats the doubled Halleluia as the title and expounds it, noting that the preceding psalm has it doubled too, the earlier being sung of Israel and this of the universal Church, and suggesting the repetition answers to the cry Abba, Father, one wall crying the one word at the corner stone and the other the other. Adam Clarke denies there is a title at all: the psalm has none in the Hebrew or in any version, and the Hallelujah prefixed to some is no title but was most probably borrowed from the close of the psalm before. Augustine also states the condition on which the psalm can be enjoyed: it commends the mercies of God proved in ourselves, and it is a wonder if it can please anyone who has not learned in his own case what he hears; it was written that the people of God might know itself in it as in a mirror.

Two describe the same architecture and credit the same critic. Clarke finds the psalm sung in parts with a double burden, one set of verses forming the cry for deliverance and another the chorus of thanksgiving, and cites a bishop’s lecture for the observation that after each intercalary verse one is added expressive of deliverance. John Calvin carries a note making the same analysis, marking that the last two burdens are separated by two verses instead of one, and quoting the same critic that the psalm is among the most elegant monuments of antiquity. Keil and Delitzsch look at position instead: the psalm opens the Fifth Book of the Psalter, and as the fifth book of the Law opens with Israel on the threshold of the promised land, so here Israel is restored to the soil of its fatherland, redeemed there out of Egypt and here out of the lands of the exile. On authorship Clarke says the author is unknown and guesses the psalm was sung, like the two before it, at the dedication of the second temple; Calvin’s note prefers David while allowing that some place it later.

Who the redeemed are divides them. John Gill excludes two candidates by argument: not the deliverance from Egypt, since they were then brought out of one land and not several, and not the Babylonish captivity, since they were not gathered from all four quarters as the verse says; so he takes it of the effectual calling and of the Gentiles. Clarke allows the historical returns under a series of kings but holds the prophecy completed only under the Gospel. Matthew Henry takes a temporal deliverance and applies it spiritually. Charles Ellicott declines to settle it: whether the wandering is an historical fact or an imaginary picture, the reference to the dangers of eastern travel is equally clear.

Ellicott finds a real crux in the third verse. The fourth quarter is named by the word for sea, which by general usage should stand for the west; since that leaves the compass incomplete, emendations have been proposed, the best a word meaning right hand and so south. But he asks whether the text may not be right after all, the phrase belonging with the four scenes of misery that follow, so that gathering out of the sea is meant literally of the men in the ships. On the wilderness C.H. Spurgeon writes the strongest lines: solitude is a great intensifier of misery, a soul without sympathy is on the borders of hell, a solitary way the way of despair. Ellicott sets a modern poet’s line about the lone and level sands beside it. Gill reads the hunger and thirst as the state of souls newly convinced; Clarke notes that the wonders celebrated are done for the undeserving, the children of Adam, the corrupt descendants of a rebel father; John Wesley keeps the gathering literal.
10:
Whose prison is this? John Gill reports that an old paraphrase applies it to the Babylonish captivity and says it is much better to read it of prisoners in common, whose cells are dark dungeons where they are deprived of the company of the living and seem already dead. Adam Clarke takes the opposite line and makes the whole passage a similitude for the captives in Babylon. Charles Ellicott argues the particular reference from the vocabulary: the word for contemning is an old designation for the provocation offered by the chosen people, so the verse is more applicable to a violation of Israel’s covenant relations than to heathen opposition. Matthew Henry keeps it general, prisoners of any age, and turns the description into a reason for prizing liberty.

Ellicott then furnishes the cell. Darkness, he notes, is a common synonym for a dungeon, and the description suits the prisons of the ancients especially, which admitted no light at all; he names a famous prison at Rome and quotes Virgil on those shut in by darkness and a blind cell. At the next verse he reads the forced labour of the eastern monarchies out of two words, rendered literally as made to bend and stumbled, so that the line becomes a picture of men staggering under the work that was the usual fate of captives. At the broken gates he adds that a prophet’s verse was in the poet’s mind, and that Virgil’s picture of the shrine of war has been compared with it.

Clarke sets out the misery as a numbered list, as he often does: they inhabit darkness and have no light, peace or prosperity; they are where death reigns and has projected his shadow; they are bound and cannot revisit the light; they are afflicted and tortured, not merely deprived; and their fetters are iron. He numbers the causes the same way: God first showed them their duty, then counselled and exhorted them, and only when lenient means proved ineffectual visited them in judgment. Henry draws the morals: those who will not be counselled cannot be helped; afflicting providences must be improved as humbling ones, and we thwart God’s design if our hearts remain as high and hard as before; and prisoners have time to pray who at liberty could find none. C.H. Spurgeon turns to actual prisons, saying that such has been the cruelty of man to man that tens of thousands have lingered in places fit only to be tombs, suffocating sepulchres where they died of broken hearts, the dread of sudden execution being the most hideous part; we should prize liberty more, he adds, if we knew by experience what fetters mean.

At the gates of brass Gill reports an interpreter calling the phrases hyperbolical, meant to express how exceeding strong the doors were, and another applying the verse to the subjection of the Roman emperors to the faith of Christ. Clarke insists the manner mattered: this was no simple deliverance but one made so as to manifest an irresistible power, the prison torn in pieces and the bars cut asunder. Henry makes the point twice over, that gates of brass could not keep God out from his people, since he was with Joseph in the prison, nor keep them in when the set time came, and that he did not put the bars back but cut them in sunder. Keil and Delitzsch stand back from the scene and read the whole strophe as one long compound subject, which is why the poet begins with participles; Ellicott makes the same grammatical observation from the other end, noting that the subject of the thanksgiving burden must be supplied from the participle at the head of the strophe, and that this bears on how the earlier burden is to be construed. John Wesley glosses the darkness in three words, as dark prisons or dungeons.
17:
They agree that the fools of this scene are not simpletons. John Gill says expressly that they are not idiots or men devoid of natural understanding but immoral persons, without the fear of God, who place their happiness in sensual enjoyments and make a mock at sin. Keil and Delitzsch make the same point grammatically, that the word is an ethical notion and not confined to the idea of defective intellect. Charles Ellicott glosses it as infatuated in wickedness, citing the ethical sense the noun bears elsewhere. Matthew Henry turns it into an argument from self-interest, sinners being fools because they wrong even their secular interest, prejudicing their health by intemperance and endangering their lives by indulging appetite. C.H. Spurgeon presses further, that they are fools still even in affliction, and that if they were brayed in a mortar with a pestle their folly would not depart.

The verb divides them, and Ellicott raises a reading that would change the whole scene. Properly, he says, the line means that they bring affliction on themselves; the Greek and the Latin have that they were humbled; and some understand it of afflicting themselves, that is of grieving for their sins, which would explain the distaste for food in the next verse as well as actual sickness would. He then rejects it on structural grounds, the analogy of the other stanzas being against putting repentance before the emphatic cry that follows. Adam Clarke corrects the English on a smaller point, that the received version does not express the clause well and should read because of the way of their transgressions; Gill and Ellicott make the same correction and inference, that the affliction follows not a single transgression but a settled course. Clarke adds that most human maladies are the fruits of sin, misery and sin being married in bonds that can never be broken.

On the loathing of food Henry writes the sharpest sentence here: those who doted most on the meat that perishes, when they come to be sick are sick of it, and the dainties they loved are loathed, so that what they took too much of they can now take nothing of. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew word for soul is commonly used of appetite, so the line might be paraphrased as their appetite turned to loathing. Clarke calls it a natural description of a sick man, appetite gone because death has seized the whole frame; Gill applies it to those whose taste is unchanged, for whom the doctrines of the Gospel are insipid; Spurgeon adds that though they lie near the gates of death they are not yet inside the sepulchre.

The healing word is read at three levels by two of them. Gill takes it of the order issued to the disease, diseases being servants that come and go at command; then of the Word made flesh, the only infallible physician; then of the Gospel, the law being the killing letter and the Gospel the means of healing. Henry does the same, applying it to the miraculous cures wrought by a word, to the spiritual cures of regeneration, and to common recoveries, where God in his providence does but speak and it is done. Ellicott keeps it plainer, that in history as in nature God’s word is his messenger, and adds that the received destructions follows the Greek while a better derivation gives pits, either metaphorically of the depths of suffering or literally of the graves the sufferers had drawn near to. On the thank-offering Clarke has them bring an innocent animal and confess that God spared them when they deserved to die; Gill will have no legal sacrifices but only spiritual ones. Gill also sets two kings against each other, one who prayed in his affliction and one who sought only to the physicians; John Wesley glosses the affliction in two words, as sickness.
23:
Nobody allegorises this scene, and Keil and Delitzsch say so, refusing an allegorical reading by name and holding that the psalm speaks of men whose calling takes them to sea, not as fishermen but in commercial enterprise. Matthew Henry supplies the sociology: the Israelites dealt little in merchandise, but their seafaring neighbours did, and this part of the psalm was perhaps calculated for them. He adds that none will expose themselves at sea but those who have business there, since among all the pleasant things of the king’s reign we read of no pleasure-boat. C.H. Spurgeon makes the same observation independently, that we never read of any man taking his pleasure on the sea, nor of the king keeping a pleasure boat, so averse was the Israelite mind to seafaring; he adds that voyages were thought of as a descent, whereas modern sailors speak of the high seas.

Two insist the description could only have been written by someone who had been there. Adam Clarke gives the longest note in the chapter to the storm, a vessel standing for a moment on the sharp ridge of a mountainous wave with a valley of frightful depth beyond and another mountain flying in the midst of heaven to submerge her as she descends; no man, he says, can form an adequate idea of it who has not been at sea in such a storm, and the raising of the vessel to the clouds and precipitating of her into the abyss seems to dissolve the very soul. Charles Ellicott reaches the same verdict about the poet, who has evidently himself been to sea and experienced the dangers he so graphically describes, and supports it with a line of Virgil about being lifted to heaven on the arched surge and sinking again to the shades, a passage of Ovid on mountains of water that seem to touch the stars, and one flat remark of his own: the recollection of seasickness is the best comment on these verses.

Henry and Ellicott quote the same proverb about the sea and prayer, and Henry turns it round: there is a saying, he reports, that those who would learn to pray should go to sea, and his own version is that those who will go to sea should learn to pray, so that they may come with more boldness to the throne of grace. Ellicott gives the proverb in Latin without comment. Henry then presses that heathen mariners in a storm cried every man to his god, but that those who have the Lord for their God are never at their faith’s end though they be at their wits’ end. John Gill supplies the heathen practice, the mariners of the fleeing prophet each crying to his own god, and with the Romans tempests themselves reckoned deities, with temples and sacrifices. Ellicott renders the wits’ end more exactly, all their wisdom swallowing itself up, and the reeling as spinning round and round.

At the calm Clarke turns to sound, saying that in the original sense and sound emphatically meet, and renders the line as a command that the whirlwind stand dumb and the billows hush. Henry has the winds fall until they only lull the waves asleep again, and takes the stilling as proof that one obeyed by winds and seas was more than a man. Ellicott notices something structural: the addition of a further verse to the refrain here, as at the end of the previous stanza, clearly points to liturgical use. Clarke ends with a scene from his own time, having often been pleased in sea-port towns to see notes sent up to the minister from sailors returning thanks for preservation from shipwreck, and asks whether that is not what the psalmist requires. John Wesley adds that the elders are the magistrates and rulers, before whom men should not be ashamed to speak of God’s works.
33:
The soil is made to answer for its inhabitants. Matthew Henry states the rule flatly: if the land be bad it is because the inhabitants are so, and justly is the ground made unfruitful to those who bring forth no fruit to God but serve another master with their corn and wine. John Gill reaches for the salt sea of the destroyed cities and the threat that the promised land should become brimstone and salt; Charles Ellicott renders the word not barrenness but a salt marsh, on the authority of the Greek and the Latin; John Wesley supplies the reason, that God does not inflict such judgments without cause but for the punishment of sin in some and its prevention in others.

Then three of them independently reach for the same modern instance. Gill says the thing is done still, this country of ours and the land in America having once been waste places and being now fruitful ones. Henry says the same at more length, that this land was formerly much of it an uncultivated desert and is now full of good things, and that the plantations in America and the colonies settled there, set against the desolations of countries in Asia and Europe that were formerly famous, expound the verse. Adam Clarke gives the fullest version and turns it into a narrative: the first colonists of any place flee a land of want that did not repay their toil, and seek a wilderness which needs only cultivation; providence so guides their steps as to lead them to rivers they can navigate and shows them wells they have not digged; there the hungry dwell, and agree for convenience and defence to build a city; they sow the fields they have cleared and plant vineyards, and their cattle are multiplied. What a fine picture, he says, of the first peopling and planting of that country, and of the divine blessing on their industry.

Henry draws the economics out of the sequence of verbs. Lands will not serve men without lodgings, and therefore they must prepare a city; lodgings will not serve without lands, and therefore they must sow and plant; and the fields, though favoured with water-springs, will yield no increase unless they are sown, so that man’s industry must attend God’s blessing and then God’s blessing will crown man’s industry. He adds that cities took rise from rising families, and that we depend on God for the increase of the cattle as much as for the increase of the ground. Gill takes the same verses spiritually, making the fields the world and the seed the word, the vineyards the churches, believers the pleasant plants in them and young converts the tender grapes.

Ellicott is meanwhile tracing where the language comes from. The dependence of this psalm on certain passages of the prophet, he says, is indubitable, but the images are used differently: the prophet thinks only of the joy of returning Israel, while here the thought is that in the reverses of fortune which even the chosen nation must be prepared for, God will intervene to protect and save. He adds that the construction becomes very awkward at the next stage because two clauses are introduced there from another book altogether. Keil and Delitzsch read the sequence as a story rather than a set of maxims, the flourishing prosperity of the settled people drawing down upon them the envy of the powerful and the tyrannical, after which God puts an end to tyranny and brings his people back to honour and strength; and they answer a critic who wished to make the turn of fortune a retrospect, on the ground that the symmetry of the continuation is against it. C.H. Spurgeon keeps to the plain reversal, that the same hand which dries the springs opens them again.
39:
Adam Clarke reads the closing verses through the wars of his own lifetime, and the commentary turns into contemporary history. At the minishing and bringing low he asks how minished and brought low the country he has just been praising was by the long and destructive war that began in one year and was not ended for eight, and what desolations have been brought on the fertile empires of Europe by the war which began in another year and did not end for twenty-two; how many millions of lives, he asks, have been sacrificed in it and souls sent unprepared into the eternal world, and when God makes inquisition for blood, on whose heads will he find the blood of these slaughtered millions. At the contempt poured upon princes he goes further and names the man: all the powers of Europe were leagued against him in vain and were as stubble to his bow, and he came, saw and conquered almost everywhere, until God destroyed his tens of thousands of veteran troops by a Russian frost, and until a particular providence intervened at the last battle when the skill and valour of his opponents had been nearly reduced to nothing. Clarke ends the note on the dreary rock of the exile.

John Wesley, without any such occasion, had glossed the same two verses in a way that fits the case exactly: the men brought low are those who, being exalted by God, grow insolent and secure, and the wandering is a banishment from their own courts and kingdoms, forcing them to flee into desolate wildernesses for shelter. John Gill keeps the register theological, God laughing at princes and having them in derision, setting them up and pulling them down at pleasure, hurling them from their thrones and making them contemptible to their own subjects; some he brings to a shameful end in this world, as the king who was eaten with worms, and those he does not will rise to everlasting contempt in the other. Clarke, at the answering verse, is careful not to overreach: the raising of the poor probably refers to the restoration from captivity, but such incidents frequently occur, and the verse is applicable to a multitude of cases.

Gill builds the lifting of the poor into a ladder. He begins with a shepherd taken from the sheepfold to be king, and then makes the poor those who are poor in purse, poor in knowledge and gifts, poor in spirit and sensible of it, and poor by reason of affliction, whom God sets among the princes of his people, and on a Rock higher than they, higher than the angels and than the heavens.

At the stopping of the mouth Clarke observes that the judgments and mercies are so distinctly marked that atheism and irreligion are confounded and the cause of falsehood made hopeless; it was only the mouth that could do anything, he says, and that only by lies, calumnies and blasphemies, and God closes it. Gill has the righteous rejoicing at the same judgments. C.H. Spurgeon makes the closing verse a rule for the reader: those who notice providences shall never be long without a providence to notice, though we must observe wisely, since otherwise we may confuse ourselves and others with hasty reflections upon the dealings of the Lord. Charles Ellicott closes with two literary observations, that the figure of families like a flock is borrowed from the book of Job, as other phrases in these verses are, and that the psalm ends in the style and almost in the very words of one of the prophets. Keil and Delitzsch, who opened the psalm with an essay on its place in the Psalter, print these last four verses and add nothing at all.
